quotes.text: The wall sit is a simple isometric leg exercise for building strength in a specific squat position, or to minimize strength loss during injuries that prevent squatting and similar.

Stand with your back to a wall and feet in front of it as far as needed for the desired squat position. Most commonly wall sits are done with 90-degree angles at the hip and knee, but other angles and depths can be used to work on specific positions.
With your back supported against the wall, slide down into the chosen squat position and hold for the prescribed time, usually 30-60 seconds.

Keep your back flat against the wall, your feet shoulder-width apart and your toes pointed slightly outward. Make sure your knees are directly above your ankles and hold the position for as long as you can.
Ensure your back and buttocks remain in contact with the wall.

The wall sit can be done for 2-5 sets of 30-60-second holds. If the athlete is able to hold for 60 seconds comfortably, variations to increase difficulty can be introduced, such as lifting one foot at a time, single-leg holds, or holding weight on the thighs.

The heart rate and blood pressure parameters produced significant inverse relationships with joint angle (r at least -0.80; P < 0.05), demonstrating that wall squat intensity can be adjusted by manipulating knee joint angle.
Sixteen participants performed a dynamic ball squat and wall squat with long HTWD and short HTWD.
patellofemoral joint force and stress were greater with a short HTWD than a long HTWD at 100° ( P = 0.007) and 90° ( P = 0.008) knee angles during squat ascent
squatting with short HTWD produced anterior knee displacement beyond the toes at higher knee angles, resulting in greater patellofemoral force and stress compared with squatting with long HTWD.
Patellofemoral force and stress were significantly greater at 90 degrees knee angle in the wall squat short compared with wall squat long

When the goal is to minimize patellofemoral compressive force and stress, it may be prudent to use a smaller knee angle range between 0 degrees and 50 degrees compared with a larger knee angle range between 60 degrees and 90 degrees
These results indicate that during isometric exercise, a breath-hold enhances an exercise-induced increase in MAP
The wall sit primarily works the quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings, and calves.
